slug: 2024-01-01 World Bank - ID4D Diagnostic of ID Systems in Cameroon

facts.fact: The World Bank's ID4D diagnostic (2023, field visit to the East region by March 2023) states that civil registration is essentially decentralised and paper-based: the registrar hand-copies each birth record six times across three paper registers, and there is no centralised, digitalised civil registry.
facts.system: Civil registration system (primary and secondary civil registration centres)

facts.fact: The diagnostic states that several partner organisations have piloted different digital systems to record births and issue digital birth certificates, while BUNEC has not yet decided on the architecture or the solution to deploy nationally; no digital recording of deaths is described.
facts.system: Partner pilot systems for recording births (including OpenCRVS)

facts.fact: The diagnostic states that digital recording of births exists only as partner pilots: GIZ and KOICA's PAMEC Phase 2 in pilot municipalities of the North, Southwest and Littoral regions, and OpenCRVS piloted by UNDP in the Far North and now by GIZ; no number of pilot offices is given, against 3,154 civil registration offices stated (374 principal, 2,522 secondary, 58 abroad).
facts.system: Partner pilot systems for recording births (including OpenCRVS)

facts.fact: The diagnostic states that the few, fragmented digitalisation efforts in civil registration have been carried out through development partners (UNDP, GIZ, KOICA, EU), using different technologies and data standards.
facts.system: Partner pilot systems for recording births (including OpenCRVS)

facts.fact: The diagnostic states that BUNEC, the national civil status office under MINDDEVEL, is tasked by the 2018 Schéma Directeur with creating a shared IT system to record births, that efforts towards a centralised BUNEC-managed registry begun in 2011 are still at an early stage, and that no clear architecture for the national database is in place.
facts.system: National civil status IT system and national civil status database (Fichier national d'état civil), planned

facts.fact: The diagnostic states that the government adopted the Civil Status Rehabilitation Strategic Plan 2018-2023 and, in 2018, the Schéma Directeur de l'Informatisation du Système National de l'État Civil, under which the digital system is to be deployed first in the main civil status centres only while secondary centres continue with paper declarations.
facts.system: National civil status IT system and national civil status database (Fichier national d'état civil), planned

facts.fact: The diagnostic states that digitalisation has been financed by development partners (the largest, GIZ and KOICA's PAMEC Phase II, about US$8 million; most others under US$2 million), that funding for nationwide scale-up of pilots has not emerged, and that a sustainable funding mechanism and a sufficient State budget allocation are lacking.
facts.system: Partner pilot systems for recording births (including OpenCRVS)

facts.fact: The diagnostic states that GIZ is now piloting OpenCRVS, the system UNDP piloted in the Far North some years earlier.

The diagnostic states that as of 2023 the steering committee of the civil registration rehabilitation programme (PRE2C, set up in 2015) is no longer active: it was financed through partner projects rather than its own budget, and stopped when those projects closed.

note: Read from the artefact PDF. The Read tool could not render the PDF (pdftoppm is not installed), so its text was extracted with pdftotext to the session scratchpad and read whole, 103 pages. The PDF is dated 2023 by its own copyright line (diagnostic begun August 2022, field visit by March 2023), not the stub's 2024-01-01. The stated office counts (374 principal, 2,522 secondary, 58 abroad) sum to 2,954, not the 3,154 stated. What the civil registration law and the 2021 draft law prescribe is left out as governance that places nothing.
